The ***Ohio* class** of [nuclear-powered submarines](Nuclear_submarine "Nuclear submarine") includes the [United States Navy](United_States_Navy "United States Navy")'s 14 [ballistic missile submarines](Ballistic_missile_submarine "Ballistic missile submarine") (SSBNs) and its four [cruise missile submarines](Cruise_missile_submarine "Cruise missile submarine") (SSGNs). Each [displacing](Displacement_(ship) "Displacement (ship)") 18,750 tons submerged, the *Ohio*-class boats are the largest submarines ever built for the U.S. Navy. They are the world's third-largest submarines, behind the [Russian Navy](Russian_Navy "Russian Navy")'s [Soviet](Soviet_Union "Soviet Union")-designed 48,000-ton [Typhoon class](Typhoon-class_submarine "Typhoon-class submarine")[[lower-alpha 2]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-11)[[10]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-12) and 24,000-ton [*Borei* class](Borei-class_submarine "Borei-class submarine").[[11]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-13) At 20 [Trident II](UGM-133_Trident_II "UGM-133 Trident II") missiles apiece, *Ohio*-class boats carry just as many missiles, if not more, than either the Borei class (16, 20 on the Borei II) or the recently deactivated *Typhoon* class (20).

Like its predecessor [*Benjamin Franklin*](Benjamin_Franklin-class_submarine "Benjamin Franklin-class submarine")- and [*Lafayette*-class](Lafayette-class_submarine "Lafayette-class submarine") subs,[[12]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChant200533-14) the *Ohio*-class SSBNs are part of the United States' [nuclear-deterrent triad](Nuclear_triad "Nuclear triad"), along with [U.S. Air Force](U.S._Air_Force "U.S. Air Force") [strategic bombers](Strategic_bomber "Strategic bomber") and [intercontinental ballistic missiles](Intercontinental_ballistic_missiles "Intercontinental ballistic missiles").[[13]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChinworth20062-15) The 14 SSBNs together carry about half of U.S. active strategic [thermonuclear](Thermonuclear_weapon "Thermonuclear weapon") warheads. The *Ohio*-class submarine was designed for extended strategic deterrent patrols. Each submarine is assigned two complete crews, called the Blue crew and the Gold crew, each typically serving 70-to-90-day deterrent patrols. To decrease the time in port for crew turnover and replenishment, three large logistics hatches have been installed to provide large-diameter resupply and repair access. These hatches allow rapid transfer of supply pallets, equipment replacement modules, and machinery components, speeding up replenishment and maintenance of the submarines. Moreover, the "stealth" ability of the submarines was significantly improved over all previous ballistic-missile subs. *Ohio* was virtually undetectable in her sea trials in 1982, giving the U.S. Navy extremely advanced flexibility.[[16]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-18)

The class's design allows the boat to operate for about 15 years between major overhauls. The *Ohio* class was designed in the 1970s to carry the concurrently designed [Trident](Trident_(missile) "Trident (missile)") [submarine-launched ballistic missile](Submarine-launched_ballistic_missile "Submarine-launched ballistic missile"). The first eight *Ohio*-class submarines were armed at first with 24 Trident I C4 SLBMs.[[6]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-Adcock_p40-6) Beginning with the ninth Trident submarine, [*Tennessee*](USS_Tennessee_(SSBN-734) "USS Tennessee (SSBN-734)"), the remaining boats were equipped with the larger, three-stage [Trident II D5 missile](Trident_missile "Trident missile").[[9]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-Adcock_p41-9) The Trident I missile carries eight [multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles](Multiple_independently_targetable_reentry_vehicle "Multiple independently targetable reentry vehicle"), while the Trident II missile carries 12, in total delivering more destructive power than the Trident I missile and with greater accuracy. Starting with [*Alaska*](USS_Alaska_(SSBN-732) "USS Alaska (SSBN-732)") in 2000, the Navy began converting its remaining ballistic missile submarines armed with C4 missiles to carry D5 missiles. This task was completed in mid-2008. The first eight submarines had their home ports at [Bangor, Washington](Naval_Base_Kitsap "Naval Base Kitsap"), to replace the submarines carrying [Polaris A3 missiles](Polaris_missile "Polaris missile") that were then being decommissioned. The remaining 10 submarines originally had their home ports at [Kings Bay, Georgia](Naval_Submarine_Base_Kings_Bay "Naval Submarine Base Kings Bay"), replacing the [Poseidon](Poseidon_missile "Poseidon missile") and Trident Backfit submarines of the Atlantic Fleet.

### SSBN/SSGN conversions

In 1994, the [Nuclear Posture Review](Nuclear_Posture_Review "Nuclear Posture Review") study determined that, of the 18 *Ohio* SSBNs the U.S. Navy would be operating in total, 14 would be sufficient for the strategic needs of the U.S. The decision was made to convert four *Ohio*-class boats into SSGNs capable of conducting conventional [land attack](Military_strike "Military strike") and [special operations](Special_forces "Special forces"). As a result, the four oldest boats of the class—*Ohio*, *Michigan*, *Florida*, and *Georgia*—progressively entered the conversion process in late 2002 and were returned to active service by 2008.[[18]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-USNF-20) The boats could thereafter carry 154 [Tomahawk cruise missiles](Tomahawk_cruise_missile "Tomahawk cruise missile") and 66 special operations personnel, among other capabilities and upgrades.[[18]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-USNF-20) The cost to refit the four boats was around US$1 billion (2008 dollars) per vessel.[[19]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-Nuclear_lives-21) During the conversion of the first four submarines to SSGNs (see below), five of the submarines, [*Pennsylvania*](USS_Pennsylvania_(SSBN-735) "USS Pennsylvania (SSBN-735)"), [*Kentucky*](USS_Kentucky_(SSBN-737) "USS Kentucky (SSBN-737)"), [*Nebraska*](USS_Nebraska_(SSBN-739) "USS Nebraska (SSBN-739)"), [*Maine*](USS_Maine_(SSBN-741) "USS Maine (SSBN-741)"), and [*Louisiana*](USS_Louisiana_(SSBN-743) "USS Louisiana (SSBN-743)"), were transferred from Kings Bay to Bangor. Further transfers occur as the strategic weapons goals of the United States change.

In 2011, *Ohio*-class submarines carried out 28 deterrent patrols. Each patrol lasts around 70 days. Four boats are on station ("hard alert") in designated patrol areas at any given time.[[20]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-22) From January to June 2014, *Pennsylvania* carried out a 140-day-long patrol, the longest to date.[[21]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-23)

The conversion modified 22 of the 24 88-inch (2.2 m) diameter Trident missile tubes to contain large [vertical launch systems](Vertical_launching_system "Vertical launching system"), one configuration of which may be a cluster of seven [Tomahawk cruise missiles](BGM-109_Tomahawk "BGM-109 Tomahawk"). In this configuration, the number of cruise missiles carried could be a maximum of 154, the equivalent of what is typically deployed in a surface battle group. Other payload possibilities include new generations of [supersonic](Supersonic "Supersonic") and [hypersonic](Hypersonic "Hypersonic") cruise missiles, and Submarine Launched Intermediate Range Ballistic Missiles,[[22]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-24) [unmanned aerial vehicles](Unmanned_aerial_vehicle "Unmanned aerial vehicle"), the [ADM-160 MALD](ADM-160_MALD "ADM-160 MALD"), sensors for antisubmarine warfare or intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions, counter mine warfare payloads such as the [AN/BLQ-11 Long Term Mine Reconnaissance System](Long-Term_Mine_Reconnaissance_System "Long-Term Mine Reconnaissance System"), and the broaching universal buoyant launcher and stealthy affordable capsule system specialized payload canisters.

The missile tubes also have room for stowage canisters that can extend the forward deployment time for special forces. The other two Trident tubes are converted to swimmer lockout chambers. For special operations, the [Advanced SEAL Delivery System](Advanced_SEAL_Delivery_System "Advanced SEAL Delivery System") and the [dry deck shelter](Dry_deck_shelter "Dry deck shelter") can be mounted on the lockout chamber and the boat will be able to host up to 66 special-operations sailors or Marines, such as [Navy SEALs](Navy_SEAL "Navy SEAL"), or [USMC](United_States_Marine_Corps "United States Marine Corps") <MARSOC> teams. Improved communications equipment installed during the upgrade allows the SSGNs to serve as a forward-deployed, clandestine Small Combatant Joint Command Center.[[23]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-25)

On 26 September 2002, the Navy awarded [General Dynamics Electric Boat](General_Dynamics_Electric_Boat "General Dynamics Electric Boat") a US$442.9 million contract to begin the first phase of the SSGN submarine conversion program. Those funds covered only the initial phase of conversion for the first two boats on the schedule. ## Replacement

Main article: [Columbia-class submarine](Columbia-class_submarine "Columbia-class submarine")

The [U.S. Department of Defense](United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") anticipates a continued need for a [sea-based strategic nuclear force](Nuclear_triad "Nuclear triad").[[45]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-GS-47) The first of the current *Ohio*-class SSBNs is expected to be retired by 2029,[[45]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-GS-47) so the replacement submarine must be seaworthy by that time. A replacement may cost over $4 billion per unit compared to *Ohio*'s $2 billion.[[3]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-Frost-3) The U.S. Navy is exploring two options. The first option is a variant of the [*Virginia*-class](Virginia-class_submarine "Virginia-class submarine") nuclear-powered attack submarines. The second option is a dedicated SSBN, either with a new hull or based on an overhaul of the current *Ohio*-class.[[46]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-48)

With the cooperation of both Electric Boat and Newport News Shipbuilding, in 2007, the U.S. Navy began a cost-control study.[[45]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-GS-47) Then in December 2008, the U.S. Navy awarded Electric Boat a contract for the missile compartment design of the *Ohio*-class replacement, worth up to $592 million. Newport News is expected to receive close to 4% of that project. In April 2009, [U.S. Defense Secretary](United_States_Secretary_of_Defense "United States Secretary of Defense") [Robert M. Gates](Robert_M._Gates "Robert M. Gates") stated that the U.S. Navy was expected to begin such a program in 2010.[[3]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-Frost-3) The new vessel was scheduled to enter the design phase by 2014. If a new hull design was to be used, the program needed to be initiated by 2016 to meet the 2029 deadline.[[45]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-GS-47)

The *Columbia*-class was officially designated on 14 December 2016, by Secretary of the Navy [Ray Mabus](Ray_Mabus "Ray Mabus"), and the lead submarine will be [USS *District of Columbia* (SSBN-826)](USS_District_of_Columbia_(SSBN-826) "USS District of Columbia (SSBN-826)").[[47]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-49) The Navy wants to procure the first *Columbia*-class boat in FY2021,[[48]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-50) though it's not expected to enter service until 2031.[[49]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-51)[[50]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-senedia.org-52)

In 2020, Navy officials first publicly discussed the idea of extending the lives of select *Ohio*-class boats at the Naval Submarine League's 2020 conference. During the 2022 conference, [Rear Admiral](Rear_admiral_(United_States) "Rear admiral (United States)") Scott Pappano, the program executive officer for strategic submarines, and Rear Admiral [Douglas G. Perry](Douglas_G._Perry "Douglas G. Perry"), the director of undersea warfare on the [Chief of Naval Operations](Chief_of_Naval_Operations "Chief of Naval Operations")' staff, discussed the *Columbia*-class program, and also touched on the possibility of finding *Ohio*-class boats that had sufficient remaining nuclear fuel and were in good enough material state to be given a further extension to their lives.[[51]](Ohio-class_submarine#cite_note-2022-11-03_DN-53)

A [state](U.S._state "U.S. state") of the [United States](United_States "United States") is one of the 50 [constituent entities](Federated_state "Federated state") that shares its [sovereignty](Sovereignty "Sovereignty") with the [federal government](Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States"). <Americans> are [citizens](Citizenship_in_the_United_States "Citizenship in the United States") of both the [federal republic](Federal_republic "Federal republic") and of the state in which they [reside](Domicile_(law) "Domicile (law)"), due to the shared sovereignty between each state and the federal government.[[1]](List_of_U.S._states_by_date_of_admission_to_the_Union#cite_note-1) <Kentucky>, <Massachusetts>, <Pennsylvania>, and <Virginia> use the [term](Nomenclature "Nomenclature") *[commonwealth](Commonwealth_(U.S._state) "Commonwealth (U.S. state)")* rather than *state* in their full official names.

States are the primary [subdivisions](Administrative_division "Administrative division") of the United States. They possess all powers not granted to the federal government, nor prohibited to them by the [Constitution of the United States](Constitution_of_the_United_States "Constitution of the United States"). In general, [state governments](State_governments_of_the_United_States "State governments of the United States") have the power to regulate issues of local concern, such as regulating intrastate commerce, running [elections](Elections_in_the_United_States "Elections in the United States"), creating [local governments](Local_government_in_the_United_States "Local government in the United States"), public school policy, and non-federal road construction and maintenance. Each state has its own [constitution](State_constitution_(United_States) "State constitution (United States)") grounded in [republican principles](Republicanism_in_the_United_States "Republicanism in the United States"), and [government](State_governments_of_the_United_States "State governments of the United States") consisting of [executive](Governor_(United_States) "Governor (United States)"), [legislative](State_legislature_(United_States) "State legislature (United States)"), and [judicial](State_court_(United_States) "State court (United States)") branches.[[2]](List_of_U.S._states_by_date_of_admission_to_the_Union#cite_note-2)

All states and their residents are represented in the federal [Congress](United_States_Congress "United States Congress"), a [bicameral](Bicameral "Bicameral") legislature consisting of the [Senate](United_States_Senate "United States Senate") and the [House of Representatives](United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives"). Each state is represented by two senators, and at least one representative, while the size of a state's House delegation depends on its total population, as determined by the most recent constitutionally mandated decennial [census](United_States_Census "United States Census").[[3]](List_of_U.S._states_by_date_of_admission_to_the_Union#cite_note-3) Additionally, each state is entitled to select a number of electors to vote in the [Electoral College](United_States_Electoral_College "United States Electoral College"), the body that elects the [President of the United States](President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") and [Vice President of the United States](Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States"), equal to the total of representatives and senators in Congress from that state.[[4]](List_of_U.S._states_by_date_of_admission_to_the_Union#cite_note-4)

[Article IV](Article_Four_of_the_United_States_Constitution "Article Four of the United States Constitution"), Section 3, Clause 1 of the Constitution grants to Congress the authority to [admit](Admission_to_the_Union "Admission to the Union") new states into the [Union](Perpetual_Union "Perpetual Union"). Since the establishment of the United States in 1776, the number of states has expanded from [the original 13](Thirteen_Colonies "Thirteen Colonies") to 50. Each new state has been admitted on an [equal footing](Equal_footing "Equal footing") with the existing states.[[5]](List_of_U.S._states_by_date_of_admission_to_the_Union#cite_note-5)

These states are presented in the order in which each [ratified](Article_Seven_of_the_United_States_Constitution "Article Seven of the United States Constitution") the 1787 Constitution and joined the others in the new (and current) federal government.
